title: Baishatun Mazu Pilgrimage
summary: No one knows where tomorrow's road will lead — not even the men carrying the palanquin. This is the only pilgrimage in Taiwan that hands the entire route over to Mazu herself, with devotees on foot following wherever she decides to go.
content:
Before dawn, in the fields of Miaoli's coastal plain, a palanquin under a pink canopy suddenly surges forward — and a few hundred pilgrims on foot instantly break into a run to keep up. No one can guess where Mazu will go next. This is the Baishatun Mazu Pilgrimage: organized by Gongtian Temple in Baishatun, Tongxiao Township, Miaoli, and heading to Chaotian Temple in Beigang, Yunlin — a round trip of about 400 km that takes 8 to 9 days, and the most legendary of all Mazu pilgrimages in Taiwan.

【No Fixed Route】
Every other Mazu procession maps out its path well in advance. Baishatun plans nothing. The whole direction is decided by Mazu's palanquin itself; the bearers only carry it, following wherever the sedan sways. That pink-canopied palanquin has earned the affectionate nickname the "Pink Supercar." Sometimes it suddenly sprints, makes a sharp turn, or even doubles back, and everyone can only stay alert and keep their eyes on it — a journey full of surprise and of moving moments. The palanquin often "charges" straight into homes, schools, and hospitals to bless the people inside, showing Mazu at her most tender and approachable.

【Sister Mazu from Shanbian】
The pilgrimage holds one especially moving detail: the Shanbian Mazu from Houlong, Miaoli rides in the very same palanquin as the Baishatun Mazu. The two have traveled together every year since 1953 — more than seventy years without a break — and are known as the "Sister Mazus," one of the gentlest chapters in Taiwan's pilgrimage culture.

【Roadside Warmth】
During these days, residents along the way set out offering tables of their own accord to greet the goddess, laying out banquet dishes, drinks, and snacks, and readying places to rest. Stranger or not, the moment they see a pilgrim they warmly wave them over to sit and eat. Many who have walked the route describe this human warmth as "the most beautiful scenery in Taiwan."

【How to Join】
Anyone can join the Baishatun Mazu Pilgrimage freely — no registration, no fee. You can walk the whole way or accompany it for just a stretch. In recent years word has spread on social media, drawing crowds of young people and foreign visitors and making it a new highlight of Taiwan's religious culture. If you can't be there in person, you can follow the palanquin's position live by GPS and take part online. The Baishatun Mazu Pilgrimage was listed as a National Important Folk Custom by the Ministry of Culture in 2010.

title: Qingshan King Festival
summary: As night falls over Wanhua, Taipei, torches and lanterns flicker on one by one and the Qingshan King's palanquin slips out on a secret night patrol — the most mysterious nighttime temple festival in northern Taiwan.
content:
On a night in the tenth lunar month, the old lanes of Wanhua, Taipei light up with torches and lanterns. The Eight Generals and the Guan Jiang Shou clear the way at the front as the Qingshan King's palanquin moves slowly into the dark alleys — this is the "night patrol" (anfang), the most mysterious nighttime temple festival in northern Taiwan. The Wanhua Qingshan King Festival is hosted by Qingshan Temple and runs for three days each year, from the 20th to the 22nd of the tenth lunar month. It ranks among Taipei's "Three Great Temple Festivals" and is northern Taiwan's most representative nighttime religious celebration.

【The Qingshan King】
The Qingshan King's given name was Zhang Gun, a county magistrate of Hui'an in the Tang Dynasty. Because he loved his people as his own children and gave his life to protect the city, he was worshipped as a deity, and his faith crossed the sea to Taiwan with migrants from Hui'an, Quanzhou. He governs justice in the underworld, going on "night patrols" to inspect the community, examine good and evil, and drive off plague and malevolent forces — a role much like that of the City God.

【Three Days of Ceremony】
● 20th of the tenth lunar month (First Night Patrol): The Qingshan King's palanquin sets out on its night inspection, with the Eight Generals, the Guan Jiang Shou, and other troupes clearing the way as it threads through Wanhua's streets, investigating the injustices of the netherworld. The nighttime procession is solemn and mysterious, and with torches and lanterns blazing together across the streets, the atmosphere is electrifying.
● 21st (Second Night Patrol): A different route is walked for a second night to make sure the whole district is protected. Local neighborhood temples send out their own troupes to join in, making the spectacle even grander.
● 22nd (Main-Day Procession): On the Qingshan King's birthday proper, the event shifts to a grand daytime procession. Palanquins, elaborately decorated performance floats (yige), troupes of every kind, and columns of devotees fill the streets of Wanhua, firecrackers thundering, in an extraordinarily lively scene.

【Distinctive Troupes】
The most eye-catching part of the festival is troupe after troupe of traditional performers: the Bajiajiang (Eight Generals) with painted faces and ritual implements in hand, the Guan Jiang Shou that originated at Dizang Temple in Xinzhuang, and Songjiang battle arrays, awakening-lion teams, and more. Each troupe has its own footwork and its own particular disciplines — a living display of Taiwanese folk art. In recent years many photography enthusiasts make the trip just to capture the drama of the night procession.

【A Modern Window】
The Qingshan King Festival holds an irreplaceable place in the hearts of Wanhua locals, and it has gradually become a window through which international visitors come to know Taiwanese temple culture. Recent editions weave in local shopping-district events, cultural-creative markets, and guided tours, letting more people discover this precious cultural heritage.

title: Wangye Worship & Welcoming King Festival
summary: Late at night on the shore at Donggang, a magnificent King Boat more than ten meters long is set alight, its flames turning the sea red — the Royal Lords are carrying away this district's plague and misfortune, returning to Heaven to report.
content:
Late at night on the shore at Donggang, Pingtung, tens of thousands of people hold their breath as a magnificent King Boat — more than ten meters long, its beams and bulwarks carved and painted — is set ablaze, the roaring flames turning the whole sea red. The Royal Lords are about to carry away this district's plague and misfortune and return to Heaven to report. This is the most stunning moment in Wangye belief. The worship of the Wangye (Royal Lords) is one of the most widespread folk faiths in southern Taiwan, and its core spirit is "patrolling on behalf of Heaven" — the Royal Lords tour the human world in Heaven's place, driving out plague while punishing evil and rewarding good. The "Welcoming King Peace Festival" is its most solemn celebration, most famously the "Donggang Welcoming King" at Donglong Temple in Donggang, Pingtung, and the "Xigang Pilgrimage" at Qing'an Temple in Xigang, Tainan.

【Where the Royal Lords Came From】
Where did the Wangye come from? Two folk explanations circulate most widely. One says the Royal Lords were originally 360 successful examination scholars of the Tang Dynasty, wrongfully killed through the schemes of a treacherous official; moved by their loyalty and righteousness, the Jade Emperor enfeoffed them as the "Thousand Years Lords who patrol on behalf of Heaven," granting them the power to inspect the human world and drive out plague. The other holds that the Wangye evolved from ancient plague-god belief — deities who once governed pestilence, later reimagined by the people as upright gods who expel it instead. Taiwan's most famous Wangye are the "Five Royal Lords" — the Lords Li, Chi, Wu, Zhu, and Fan — with Nankunshen Daitian Temple in Tainan as their head temple.

【The Donggang Welcoming King Peace Festival】
The Donggang Welcoming King is the largest Wangye festival in Taiwan, held only once every three years (a "once-in-three-years rite") and running for eight days and seven nights:
● Day One, "Inviting the Water": The Royal Lords are welcomed ashore at the Donggang seaside. Ritual masters set up an altar by the sea to reverently invite the Thousand Years Lords who patrol for Heaven to descend, and the palanquins charge back and forth at the water's edge in a breathtaking scene.
● The Middle Days, "Procession and Inspection": The Royal Lords' palanquins tour Donggang's seven jiaotou (its seven administrative districts). At each stop residents lay out offering tables and abundant offerings to greet them, and every district's troupes — the Eight Generals, Songjiang arrays, the Seventh and Eighth Lords, and more — turn out in full force amid thundering gongs and drums.
● The Final Day, "Sending Off the King" (Burning the King Boat): the climax of the entire festival. Devotees work together to build an exquisite, magnificent King Boat, its hull more than ten meters long with carved beams and painted panels, loaded with "provisioning goods" — miniature models of grain, clothing, furniture, and other daily necessities for the Royal Lords to take back to Heaven. The sending-off is held in the dead of night, with tens of thousands of devotees gathered on the shore; once the ritual masters finish chanting the scriptures, the King Boat is lit. The fierce blaze swallows the ornate hull, a sign that the Royal Lords have taken the plague and misfortune away with them and returned to Heaven to report, the firelight reflecting off the sea in an awe-inspiring, overwhelming spectacle. The Donggang Welcoming King has been listed as a National Important Folk Custom.

【The Xigang Pilgrimage】
The Xigang Pilgrimage is as renowned as the Donggang Welcoming King and is likewise held once every three years, though in a different form. The Xigang Pilgrimage is celebrated for its "troupe" (zhentou) culture: the Songjiang arrays, lion arrays, dragon arrays, and other martial-arts troupes in its procession give superb performances, earning it the title "Taiwan's Number One Pilgrimage." It, too, has been listed as a National Important Folk Custom.

【Nankunshen Daitian Temple】
Nankunshen Daitian Temple in Tainan is honored as the "head temple of the Wangye." Its great festival in the late fourth lunar month each year draws millions of worshippers. The temple carries a famous legend of a "contest of magic" between the Five Royal Lords and the Wanshan Shrine (the "Child Lord") — a dispute finally mediated by the Bodhisattva Guanyin, who brought the Royal Lords and the Child Lord to coexist in peace, a story that has become Nankunshen's most celebrated point of faith.

title: Lunar New Year Customs
summary: A dab of malt sugar smeared on the Kitchen God's lips, just to coax him into putting in a few good words up in Heaven — from the year-end feast to the first day back at work, every Lunar New Year custom in Taiwan hides a blessing behind it.
content:
On the day the gods are seen off, the woman of the house smears a dab of sweet malt sugar on the Kitchen God's lips, hoping he will put in a few extra good words for the family up in Heaven — the first delicate gesture of the Taiwanese New Year. The Lunar New Year is Taiwan's most important traditional festival, and its string of preparations and customs begins as early as the twelfth lunar month, each step holding a deep blessing and layers of cultural meaning.

【Getting Ready】
Preparations open on the 16th of the twelfth lunar month with the weiya, the year-end feast at which bosses treat their staff to thank them for a year of hard work. Then comes the 24th, the "Seeing Off the Gods" day, when the Kitchen God ascends to Heaven to report to the Jade Emperor on how the family has behaved all year — hence the custom of smearing malt sugar on his lips so he will "carry only sweet words to Heaven." A week before New Year's Eve the big clean-up begins, called "sweeping the dust," symbolically clearing out the old year's bad luck to welcome the spring. Every household stocks up on festive goods, and New Year markets like Taipei's Dihua Street throng with crowds, the holiday spirit thick in the air.

【The Reunion Dinner】
On New Year's Eve the whole family gathers for the reunion dinner, called weilu, "gathering around the stove" — traditionally a charcoal brazier was placed under the table to symbolize the family reunited, warm and thriving. The table always holds auspicious dishes: long-leaf mustard greens (kept whole and uncut) for "longevity"; fish for "surplus year after year" (and it must not be finished — some is left until the first day to make the surplus real); radish (caitou) for "good fortune"; rice cake (niangao) for "rising higher step by step"; and dumplings, shaped like gold ingots, for "bringing in wealth and treasure." Today a hot pot around the table is the most common form the reunion dinner takes in Taiwanese homes.

【Red Envelopes and Staying Up】
On New Year's Eve or the first morning, elders give yasui money to the young in red envelopes, the red packet holding joy and blessing. "Yasui" originally meant "to suppress evil spirits" (sui, "evil," being a homophone of sui, "year"), a wish to keep children safe as they grow. Amounts favor even or lucky numbers (such as 600, 1,200, or 2,000) and avoid 4. Married adults also give red envelopes to honor their parents and elders. Once the envelopes are handed out, the family "keeps the year" together — staying up late through the night, which is said to add years to one's parents' lives.

【Couplets and Decorations】
Red couplets bearing auspicious phrases are pasted on both sides of the main door, usually put up just before New Year's Eve, their words mostly praying for a peaceful new year and flowing wealth. The character for "spring" or "fortune" is pasted upside down on the door, playing on the fact that "upside down" (dao) sounds like "arrived" (dao) — so "spring has arrived," "fortune has arrived." Red paper cuttings decorate the windows, and firecracker-shaped ornaments and red lanterns hang at the doorway, joy everywhere you look.

【Customs from the First to the Fifth Day】
● Day 1: Put on new clothes and go "spring visiting" to wish everyone a happy new year; head to the temples to compete for the first incense of the year. Avoid sweeping the floor (lest you sweep away your wealth) and breaking bowls or plates (and if one does break, quickly say "peace year after year").
● Day 2: Married daughters return to their parents' home, bringing their husbands and gifts to visit — the liveliest day of the year for the maternal family.
● Day 3: the "Red Dog Day," traditionally an unlucky day for visiting; it is also the day of the "mice marrying off their daughters," so people turn off the lights and go to bed early.
● Day 4: "Welcoming the Gods" day, greeting the deities back from Heaven to their posts on earth, with temples holding welcoming ceremonies.
● Day 5: the "reopening" day (kaigong), when shops open for business and set off firecrackers to welcome the God of Wealth, and workers return to their jobs.

【Other New Year Elements】
Festive flowers (narcissus, orchids, pussy willow, plum blossom), firecrackers, dragon and lion dances, and spring visiting — along with lighting "bright-light" lamps at the temple and "securing Taisui" for the year — are all indispensable parts of the Taiwanese Lunar New Year. During the holiday temples also hand out "wealth money" and "peace talismans," with devotees lining up for a lucky start to the new year.

title: Dajia Mazu Pilgrimage
summary: The baomazi walks at the very front — one foot in a straw sandal, the other bare — striking a bronze gong to tell everyone along the road: Mazu is coming. Nine days, eight nights, 340 kilometers, and millions walking behind.
content:
At the very head of the procession walks a man in a bamboo hat and short jacket, a dry-tobacco pipe in his mouth and reading glasses on his nose, one foot in a straw sandal and the other bare, striking a bronze gong as he goes — he is the baomazi, whose job is to tell residents along the road in advance: Mazu is coming. This is the Dajia Mazu Pilgrimage, the most iconic religious event in Taiwan. Every year in the third lunar month the procession sets out from Jenn Lann Temple in Dajia, Taichung, bound for Fengtian Temple in Xingang, Chiayi — a round trip of about 340 km walked over nine days and eight nights, passing through the four counties and cities of Taichung, Changhua, Yunlin, and Chiayi and more than a hundred temples. Discovery Channel once named it one of the world's three great religious events (alongside Christmas Mass at the Vatican and the Hajj to Mecca), and each year it draws millions of participants — one of Taiwan's most precious pieces of cultural heritage.

【Route and Itinerary】
The procession departs from Jenn Lann Temple in Dajia, Taichung and makes its way through Qingshui, Shalu, Changhua, Xiluo, and Xingang, reaching as far as Fengtian Temple in Xingang, Chiayi, where it performs the "dividing of the incense fire" (huihuo) before turning back. The full journey is about 340 km over nine days and eight nights. Setting out before dawn each day, it winds along country lanes and through town streets, greeted by hundreds of temples that set up stops to host and honor the goddess along the way. The route is broadly fixed but adjusted slightly each year, with towns everywhere vying to have Mazu stop and stay — a lively affair.

【Who Walks in the Procession】
The procession is vast and highly ordered, and every role has its own history and function:
● Baomazi: the scout at the very front, in his distinctive get-up (bamboo hat, short jacket, dry-tobacco pipe in the mouth, reading glasses on the nose), one foot in a straw sandal and the other bare, striking a bronze gong as he walks to warn residents ahead that Mazu is about to arrive.
● Head Banner, Head Lantern, and Three-Immortals Banners: the ceremonial vanguard that announces the arrival of Mazu's sacred presence.
● The Thirty-Six Attendants: an honor guard bearing an array of ceremonial weapons, symbolizing Mazu's grandeur and dignity.
● Embroidered-Banner Teams: made up of devotees from many places, each carrying banners embroidered with the names of their temples.
● The Zhuangyi Troupe and Big-Drum Array: keeping order in the procession and clearing the way with gongs and drums.
● The Palanquin Bearers: the heart of the procession, shouldering Mazu's palanquin forward.

【Passing Under the Palanquin】
"Passing under the palanquin" (zuan jiaojiao) is the moment devotees most look forward to in the Dajia Mazu Pilgrimage — people kneel and press themselves to the ground so that Mazu's palanquin passes over their heads, praying to ward off disaster and win peace and good fortune. As the palanquin nears, devotees kneel down along the roadside one after another, forming a human line stretching hundreds of meters — a magnificent sight. Man or woman, old or young, whatever one's status, everyone bows in equal, earnest prayer before Mazu.

【Roadside Warmth】
During these days, residents along the way set out offering tables of their own accord to greet the goddess, laying out abundant offerings and readying free banquet food, drinks, snacks, boxed meals, and places to rest. Stranger or not, they warmly call devotees over to "sit and eat" — a genuine human warmth that many describe as "the most beautiful scenery in Taiwan." Some shops along the route even close for several days to devote themselves entirely to hosting.

【Joining Today】
Anyone can join the Dajia Mazu Pilgrimage freely — no registration, no fee. You can walk the whole way (following all nine days and eight nights), accompany it for just a stretch, or greet it at a fixed point along the route. In recent years, spread by social media, it has drawn crowds of young people and foreign travelers, becoming an international highlight of Taiwan's religious culture. During the pilgrimage you can also track the palanquin's position live by GPS. The Dajia Mazu Pilgrimage was designated a National Important Folk Custom in 2008.

title: Yanshui Beehive Fireworks
summary: The moment the palanquin halts before a fort of fireworks, tens of thousands of bottle rockets explode at once, the sparks pouring out like a swarm of bees bursting from the hive — and devotees firmly believe that the more rockets strike you, the better your luck in the year to come.
content:
The palanquin halts before the "beehive fort," a stick of incense touches the fuse, and in an instant tens of thousands of bottle rockets explode all at once, sparks flying in every direction like a whole hive of bees bursting out — and that is exactly where the name "beehive fireworks" (fengpao) comes from. The Yanshui Beehive Fireworks is a large folk event held every Lantern Festival (the 15th of the first lunar month) in Yanshui District, Tainan. Together with the Pingxi Sky Lanterns it forms the famous pairing "beehive fireworks in the south, sky lanterns in the north," and it is Taiwan's most thrilling and hair-raising folk celebration, hailed as one of the "world's three great folk festivals."

【The Legend of Its Origin】
The origins of the Yanshui Beehive Fireworks reach back to the Guangxu era of the Qing Dynasty. As the story goes, plague was ravaging the Yanshui area at the time, the dead and stricken beyond counting, and the residents were at a loss. Someone proposed inviting Guan Sheng Di Jun from the Martial Temple to process through the streets, setting off great quantities of firecrackers along the way to drive out the plague and its evil forces. The palanquin processed for three straight days, from the 13th of the first lunar month to the Lantern Festival night of the 15th, the fireworks never ceasing — and, as if by miracle, the plague gradually faded after the Lantern Festival. From then on the people of Yanshui have carried on the tradition every Lantern Festival, both to thank Guan Sheng Di Jun for delivering them from the plague and to pray for a safe and smooth year ahead.

【Building the Fireworks Fort】
At the heart of the event is the "beehive fort" (paocheng) — tens of thousands of bottle rockets (small rocket fireworks) tied to wooden or metal frames and arranged into a giant castle-shaped battery. Each fort stands about two to four meters tall, the large ones over six meters, holding anywhere from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of rockets. The forts are often lavishly decorated — some shaped as dragons and phoenixes, others inscribed with shop names and auspicious phrases. The rockets' fuses are strung together with incense sticks, so that once lit, thousands fire at once, sparks scattering like a swarming hive — hence the name "beehive fireworks." Dozens of forts may be set off in a single night, the blasts deafening and the spectacle overwhelming.

【How the Night Unfolds】
On the afternoon of the Lantern Festival, the palanquins of Guan Sheng Di Jun and the deities Zhou Cang and Guan Ping set out in turn from the Martial Temple. The procession, led by the baomazi, the head banner, and the divine-general troupes, threads through the old streets of Yanshui. Each time a palanquin arrives before a fort, the fort's owner first offers incense and lights candles, and once the palanquin is in position the fort is ignited — in an instant thousands of rockets fire together, sparks bursting everywhere, the whole street swallowed in smoke and flame. The accompanying "rocket-plowing" teams (fully armored devotees) charge straight into the heart of the fireworks, taking the beehive's baptism with their own bodies — for devotees firmly believe that the more rockets strike them, the more their fortune will flourish in the coming year. The event runs from dusk deep into the night, sometimes not ending until the early hours.

【Protective Gear】
To take part in the beehive fireworks, you must armor up thoroughly: heavy cotton clothing over the whole body (long sleeves and long trousers — avoid synthetics, which melt and cause burns), a full-face helmet (with goggles or a visor), a wet towel around the neck, thick gloves, and closed, covering shoes. Even fully geared up, getting hit by rockets is routine — but devotees welcome it gladly. "The fiercer, the more prosperous" is the singular spirit of faith behind the Yanshui Beehive Fireworks.

【Preservation and Tourism】
The Yanshui Beehive Fireworks was chosen in 2013 as one of the "Top 100 Religious Sceneries of Taiwan," and each year it draws hundreds of thousands of visitors from home and abroad to experience it. In recent years the local government has tightened safety controls — marking off restricted zones and deploying extra firefighters and medical staff — while pairing the event with cultural and historical tours of Yanshui's old streets, keeping this traditional folk custom just as thrilling but far safer.

title: Zhongyuan Ghost Festival
summary: On the first day of the seventh lunar month, King Yama opens the gates of the underworld and lets the spirits return to the world of the living — and for a whole month, Taiwanese lay out offering tables and softly call them "good brothers," folding both reverence and tenderness into every small detail.
content:
On the first day of the seventh lunar month, folk belief says that King Yama opens the gates of the underworld to let the spirits return and enjoy the offerings of the living, until the ghost gate closes again on the 30th. For this whole month, Taiwanese lay out offering tables and softly call the spirits "good brothers," folding both reverence and tenderness into every small detail. The Zhongyuan Pudu (the universal salvation of the Ghost Festival) is the most important sacrificial event of Taiwan's seventh lunar month, and the largest and most distinctive Ghost Month tradition in folk belief.

【Ghost Month Customs and Taboos】
The seventh lunar month carries a heavy folk atmosphere in Taiwan. On the first day, the "opening of the ghost gate," temples hold rites such as "opening the niche gate" or "raising the lantern pole" to let the good brothers (a respectful term for the spirits) know they may return to the human world. Many taboos circulate through the month:
● Don't swim at night — water ghosts seek substitutes to take their place.
● Don't hang laundry out at night — the shape of the clothes resembles a human form and easily draws spirits to attach themselves.
● Don't whistle — the sound will call the good brothers to you.
● Don't tap someone on the shoulder — a person carries a protective "true flame" on each shoulder and on the crown of the head, and a tap can snuff one out, leaving them vulnerable.
● Don't say the word "ghost" — use the respectful "good brothers" instead.
● Avoid major undertakings such as moving house, opening a business, or marrying.
Modern people may not follow every rule, but these ideas remain deeply rooted in Taiwanese society.

【How the Pudu Unfolds】
The 15th day, Zhongyuan proper, is the peak of the pudu. Households set up offering tables at their doors or under the arcade, laid with abundant "three sacrifices" (pork, chicken, fish), fruit, snacks, drinks, and instant noodles — modern Taiwanese pudu spreads grow ever more lavish, with some even offering whole cases of beer and all kinds of imported treats. Incense is planted in the offerings, and gold and silver spirit money is burned for the good brothers to use. The table must include a paper image of the "Pudu Lord" (the Burning-Face Great Being, also called Da Shi Ye), an incarnation of Guanyin who keeps order during the pudu so the good brothers do not fight over the offerings.

【Offering Taboos】
● Don't stand chopsticks upright in the rice — that is the "foot-of-the-bed rice" offered to the dead.
● Offerings for the good brothers should be more lavish than those for the gods — a show of generosity, lest the good brothers be displeased.
● Don't include guava or tomato — the ancients regarded these two fruits, whose seeds pass through and out of the body, as "unclean."
● After the pudu, the offerings are best taken back and eaten soon rather than left out for long.

【Major Zhongyuan Celebrations】
Taiwan's grandest Zhongyuan festival is the "Keelung Ghost Festival," running a full month from the "opening of the niche gate" on the first of the seventh lunar month to the "closing of the niche gate" at month's end. Its core activities include raising the lantern pole (to summon the lonely souls of land and water), the main altar rites (with eleven surnames taking turns to host), the release of water lanterns (lotus-shaped lanterns floated on the Keelung River to guide the spirits in the water to come and receive the offerings — a hauntingly beautiful and spectacular sight), and parade floats (elaborate decorated tableaux built by each surname group). The Keelung Ghost Festival has over 170 years of history, is listed as a National Important Folk Custom, and draws hundreds of thousands of visitors each year.

【Grabbing the Lonely-Ghost Offerings】
"Qianggu" (grabbing the lonely-ghost offerings) is the most heart-stopping part of the Zhongyuan Pudu, most famous at Toucheng in Yilan. After the pudu rites end, several tall "lonely-ghost platforms" (some ten-odd meters high), their poles slathered in beef tallow, are raised in the square, with offerings and flags set at the top. Competing teams must climb the slick poles bare-handed to seize the flags and offerings at the summit. Whoever grabs the "fair-wind flag" is believed to win the blessing of the good brothers. Combining athletic contest with religious meaning, it is one of the most singular parts of Taiwan's Zhongyuan culture.

title: Lantern Festival
summary: Thousands of sky lanterns rise all at once, carrying people's wishes up into the night like a sky full of slowly drifting stars — this is the Lantern Festival, the last night of the Lunar New Year.
content:
Night settles over Pingxi in New Taipei, and thousands of sky lanterns rise all at once, each carrying a wish written stroke by stroke, drifting slowly upward like a sky full of moving stars. This is the Lantern Festival — the 15th of the first lunar month, and the last night of the Lunar New Year, also called the "Little New Year" or the Shangyuan Festival. The day brings traditional customs of eating tangyuan, admiring lanterns, and guessing lantern riddles, and grand celebrations are held all over. The Lantern Festival is also the first of Daoism's "Three Origins Festivals" — the Shangyuan Festival, the birthday of the Heavenly Official — and folk belief holds that the Heavenly Official descends to the human world this day to bestow blessings, hence the saying "Shangyuan bestows fortune."

【Pingxi Sky Lanterns】
The releasing of sky lanterns in Pingxi District, New Taipei is the most romantic sight of the Lantern Festival. Thousands of lanterns rise together, their points of light drifting slowly up the night sky like stars, a magnificent scene. Each lantern is inscribed with people's wishes and prayers, carried skyward as a symbol of those hopes reaching Heaven. The origin of the Pingxi sky lanterns is said to trace back to Qing-era residents of these hill villages, who once released the lanterns to signal down the mountain that all was safe — a practice that later grew into the Lantern Festival wishing tradition. The Pingxi Sky Lantern Festival has been ranked by CNN among "the 52 best fresh things worth doing in the world" and listed by National Geographic among the "world's top ten winter travel destinations."

【The Taiwan Lantern Festival】
The Taiwan Lantern Festival is a major annual event hosted by the Tourism Administration of the Ministry of Transportation and Communications, held since 1990 in a different county or city each year. Its main lantern takes the year's zodiac animal as its theme, often reaching tens of meters tall, and is joined by lantern displays of every kind, technology and art lantern zones, international exchange zones, and performances, over a run of about two weeks. The festival's scale and artistry have risen year after year, in recent editions incorporating LED technology, projection mapping, and interactive installation art, drawing millions of visitors from home and abroad and becoming a major brand of Taiwanese tourism.

【Distinctive Local Celebrations】
Beyond "beehive fireworks in the south, sky lanterns in the north," many unique Lantern Festival events take place across Taiwan:
● Bombing Master Handan in Taitung: devotees hurl firecrackers at the bare-chested, flesh-and-blood Master Handan (played by a real person who stands on a palanquin and bears the barrage), a heart-stopping scene. Master Handan is seen as an incarnation of the God of Wealth, and the fiercer the bombing, the more prosperous the year to come.
● Bombing the Dragon in Miaoli (Bang Long): firecrackers are hurled to "bomb" the dragon-dance teams as they weave and soar amid the dense bursts of firelight, symbolizing the dragon's might and auspiciousness — now listed as an important Hakka cultural celebration.
● Luermen Fireworks in Tainan: a high-altitude fireworks show held by the Orthodox Luermen Shengmu Temple, joining Mazu culture with the Lantern Festival.
● Yeliu Deity-Palanquin Harbor Crossing: fishermen in Yeliu, Wanli District shoulder deity palanquins and leap into the frigid sea to process through the water, praying for safety at sea and a bountiful catch — the "bravest" Lantern Festival event in all Taiwan.

【Festival Foods and Culture】
On the Lantern Festival people eat tangyuan (glutinous rice balls), for the meaning of "roundness and reunion." Taiwanese tangyuan are mostly filled with peanut, sesame, or red bean, and there are savory versions too (the Hakka savory tangyuan with crown daisy greens is especially famous). The Lantern Festival is also one of the traditional "Chinese Valentine's Days" — in the old days women could seldom go out, and lantern-viewing on this night was a rare chance to do so, so that many gifted scholars and fair maidens met at the lantern displays and made lasting matches. "In the crowd I sought her a thousand times; suddenly I turned, and there she was, where the lantern lights were growing dim" captures the most moving image of a Lantern Festival night.

title: Jiao Festival (Community Purification Ritual)
summary: For days on end the whole village takes no life and touches no meat — markets stop selling fish and pork, and even the convenience stores pull meat products from the shelves. This is the Jiao Festival, the grandest and most devout community rite in Taiwan.
content:
During a Jiao Festival, the whole village takes no life and touches no meat for days on end: markets stop selling fish and pork, restaurants switch to vegetarian fare, and even the nearby convenience stores pull their meat products from the shelves. This collective devotion is the very thing that most astonishes outsiders. The Jiao Festival (jianjiao) is the largest and most solemn community religious ceremony in Taiwanese folk belief. Also called "doing the Jiao" or "striking the Jiao," it is held only once every three, five, twelve, or even several dozen years; throughout the festival everyone within the designated area keeps a vegetarian fast, forbids slaughter, and erects altars to pray for peace — a vital tradition that binds a community together.

【What Is a Jiao Festival?】
The character jiao originally meant "a sacrifice to the heavenly gods." A Jiao Festival is led by the local temple and presided over by a troupe of Daoist priests, a large-scale liturgical ceremony whose core purposes are to thank the gods for their protection, pray for peace across the whole community, and deliver the souls of the wandering dead — carrying the sense of "repaying Heaven's grace and praying for blessing." A complete Jiao usually lasts three to seven days (called a "Three-Morning Jiao," "Five-Morning Jiao," or "Seven-Morning Jiao"); the longer the Jiao, the greater its scale and the more considerable the manpower and resources it demands.

【Types of Jiao Festivals】
● Qing'an Jiao (Peace-Praying Jiao): the most common type, focused on praying for peace and safety throughout the community.
● Qingcheng Jiao (Completion Jiao): held when a temple is newly built or restored, combining celebration with prayers for peace.
● Wen Jiao (Plague Jiao): performed to drive out pestilence, originating in the ancient plague-sending rites.
● Shui Jiao (Water Jiao): held in areas prone to water accidents, praying for safety on the waterways.
● Huo Jiao (Fire Jiao): held to pray for protection from the disaster of fire.

【Fasting and Taboos】
During the Jiao Festival, the whole jiao domain (the area the festival covers) enforces a strict "ban on slaughter and vegetarian fast" — every resident and business must eat vegetarian, take no life, and consume no meat. Markets stop selling fish and pork, restaurants turn to vegetarian menus, and even the nearby convenience stores cooperate by pulling their meat products. This strictness often leaves outsiders in awe, yet to the locals it is devotion taken entirely for granted. Within the jiao domain, "earth-disturbing" acts such as weddings and moving house are also forbidden, preserving a solemn and reverent atmosphere.

【Altars and Rites】
Several temporary altars are raised during the Jiao: the "Heavenly Altar," for worshipping the Three Pure Ones and the Jade Emperor, is the highest tier; the "Earth Altar," set on the ground, is for delivering the souls of the dead; and the "Water Altar," placed by the water, delivers the spirits of the drowned. The Daoist priests, in elaborate ritual vestments, perform rites day and night without pause — the morning audience with Heaven at dawn, the noon offering, the release of water lanterns at night to guide the dead across, the universal feeding of the hungry ghosts, and the closing thanksgiving that brings it to a perfect end. The whole process follows a rigorous ritual sequence, the priests' chanting, ritual footwork, and instrument-playing weaving together into solemn yet magnificent religious music.

【Famous Jiao Festivals】
Taiwan's most renowned Jiao Festivals include the Keelung Ghost Festival (held annually, the largest Zhongyuan celebration in all Taiwan), the Tainan Yanshui Grand Jiao, the Jiao of Lugang Tianhou Temple in Changhua, and the Jiao of Beigang Chaotian Temple in Yunlin. The Keelung Ghost Festival, which combines clan-rotation hosting, parade floats, and the release of water lanterns, has been listed as a National Important Folk Custom. In late 2024, the "Three-Morning Completion Thanksgiving Peace Jiao" held at Dalongdong Baoan Temple in Taipei was a major event unseen in over thirty years, with the entire district keeping the fast and slaughter ban and tens of thousands taking part.

【Community Solidarity】
The most precious meaning of a Jiao Festival lies in the collective mobilization of the whole community. From the preparation stage onward, residents divide the work — some raise the altars, some cook the vegetarian banquets, some patrol to keep order, some handle the fundraising. The "thanksgiving banquet" after the ceremony (also called the "peace banquet") is a grand reunion of the whole village, with hundreds of tables of vegetarian feast prepared by professional outdoor banquet chefs (zongpushi), embodying the community's deepest bonds of fellowship and shared identity.
